periods.analysis: College & Career Readiness opened the arc at 54.1%, which keeps Harborview in yellow: within reach of the 60% target, but not yet where our students deserve to be. The strongest signals came from the Harborview Technical Pathways programs at Seaport High and Northgate Academy, where dual-enrollment welding, logistics, and aviation-maintenance seats filled quickly around the airport and port employer partnerships. The watch-item is that readiness is still being held down by uneven Algebra II credit completion and FAFSA/financial-aid documentation gaps among seniors who were otherwise on track. I read this as a solid base, not a plateau, and it calls for disciplined follow-through rather than a new slogan.
periods.recommendations: Keep the yellow status in active management by expanding senior transcript audits to every high school advisory section by the sixth week of the term. Sustain what is working by protecting the Port-to-Pathways employer rotations and adding a second FAFSA completion night at Central, East Harbor, and Seaport High. Direct principals to produce a named-student list for every senior within one requirement of readiness, with counselor follow-up logged weekly.

periods.analysis: The measure slipped from 54.1% to 53.3%, a quarter-over-quarter movement of -0.8, so I am watchful but not surprised. Quarter four exposed the predictable friction points: winter attendance interruptions, midyear credit recovery starts that came too late for some students, and incomplete industry-certification testing windows in the health sciences and maritime cohorts. The number remains yellow, above the red threshold but still materially short of the >=60% target. The important lesson is that readiness cannot be treated as a senior-year rescue operation; the pipeline has to be managed earlier and by name.
periods.recommendations: Move the readiness review upstream by requiring 10th- and 11th-grade on-track conferences before spring course requests are finalized. Add Saturday certification labs for CNA, CompTIA, and OSHA-10 candidates at Harborview Career Center, with transportation from the Route 4 and Route 11 school-bus corridors. Ask each high school to report weekly on students missing only assessment, credit, or documentation components so the district can separate true academic gaps from paperwork delays.

periods.analysis: We regained a small amount of ground, moving from 53.3% to 53.7%, a quarter-over-quarter increase of 0.4. That is not celebration-level movement, but it tells me the January counselor blitz, the FAFSA clinics at the East Harbor Library branch, and the first wave of credit-recovery completions are beginning to register. The status remains yellow because 53.7% is still below the 60% target, and the margin is too wide to close through end-of-year activity alone. The watch-item is chronic absenteeism among juniors in the Bayside and Airport corridor attendance zones, because readiness indicators weaken quickly when students miss lab days and gateway math instruction.
periods.recommendations: Continue the counselor blitz, but narrow it to students who can realistically convert this semester through one course, one assessment, or one certification. Pair attendance outreach with readiness advising by assigning success coaches to the junior cohorts at Bayside, East Harbor, and Seaport High. Sustain the library-based financial-aid clinics and add employer volunteers from Harborview International Airport and Pier 6 logistics firms to help families connect paperwork to real postsecondary options.

periods.analysis: The measure improved from 53.7% to 54.2%, a quarter-over-quarter movement of +0.5, marking the second consecutive gain. This is the kind of modest, earned progress that comes from doing the ordinary work well: transcript cleanup, targeted credit recovery, certification retesting, and dual-enrollment advising before students disappear into summer schedules. We are still yellow at 54.2%, and I want us to be honest that the 60% target remains a real stretch without stronger 11th-grade course-taking patterns. The watch-item is capacity in the summer bridge sections, especially Algebra II readiness and English 11 recovery, because those seats determine whether the fall senior cohort starts close or starts behind.
periods.recommendations: Lock summer bridge rosters now and reserve seats first for students within one readiness indicator of meeting the standard. Extend the successful certification retest model into July, using Harborview Career Center labs on Tuesdays and Thursdays rather than waiting for fall. Require each principal to submit a fall senior readiness roster by pathway: college credit, career certification, military enlistment readiness, and work-based learning.

periods.analysis: College & Career Readiness held flat at 54.2%, with a quarter-over-quarter movement of 0. That steadiness is better than a summer slide, and it suggests the bridge programs and certification retests helped us protect the gains from Q1 and Q2. Still, flat yellow is not good enough when the target is >=60%, and a stable gap is still a gap. The watch-item now shifts to conversion: too many students are participating in pathway activities without completing the final credential, exam score, dual-credit transcript, or enlistment documentation that turns activity into readiness.
periods.recommendations: Run a 45-day conversion campaign focused only on unfinished readiness artifacts: AP/dual-credit transcript posting, industry exam retakes, ASVAB documentation, and work-based learning verification. Sustain summer bridge gains by scheduling fall check-ins for every completer before the first interim grading period. Have the district data team reconcile vendor files from Certiport, NCCER, College Board, and the community college so schools are not chasing students who have already met the requirement.

periods.analysis: The rate moved down from 54.2% to 53.7%, a quarter-over-quarter change of -0.5, returning us to the level we saw in 2025-Q1. I am concerned by the backslide, but it is a managed concern because the underlying reviews show identifiable issues: late dual-credit transcript imports from Harborview Community College, missed fall retest windows, and absenteeism spikes in the senior cohort during storm-disrupted weeks. The measure remains yellow, not red, yet the pattern tells us that small gains are fragile when operational handoffs are loose. We cannot allow a student who has done the work to be invisible in the data, and we cannot allow a student who is one step away to drift through the holidays.
periods.recommendations: Stand up a December Readiness War Room with counseling, assessment, CTE, and data staff reviewing one named-student roster twice weekly. Prioritize correction of dual-credit and certification records before launching new interventions, because clean data will tell us who truly needs help. Assign winter-break outreach to seniors with one missing readiness component, and use school-based family liaisons for students with attendance barriers in the Tidegate and South Harbor neighborhoods.

periods.analysis: We recovered from 53.7% to 54.1%, a quarter-over-quarter increase of +0.4. That improvement suggests the December Readiness War Room and data reconciliation work found students who had earned readiness but were not yet counted, while also pushing some one-step-away seniors across the line. Even so, 54.1% remains yellow and below the >=60% target, so I do not want anyone mistaking recovery for acceleration. The watch-item is whether we can move from cleanup to earlier preparation, especially for juniors whose math sequence, attendance pattern, or lack of a pathway concentration already signals risk.
periods.recommendations: Keep the Readiness War Room through the end of the school year, but add a junior dashboard so the work is preventive rather than only corrective. Extend the family-liaison model to March and April attendance recovery, with counselors tying attendance plans to specific readiness milestones. Sustain the data reconciliation process by setting monthly file-matching dates with Harborview Community College, Certiport, NCCER, and the military recruitment partners.

periods.analysis: The measure rose from 54.1% to 55.3%, a quarter-over-quarter gain of +1.2, our strongest movement in this eight-quarter run. We are still yellow because 55.3% remains below the 60% target, but this is the first quarter that feels like genuine acceleration rather than maintenance. The gains appear tied to earlier junior advising, cleaner vendor-file matching, expanded certification retesting, and better senior follow-through in the aviation, health sciences, logistics, and information technology pathways. My watch-item is sustainability: a strong Q2 can fade if summer course access, transportation, and credential testing are not locked before students leave campus.
periods.recommendations: Treat the +1.2 gain as a model to scale, not a reason to relax: preserve the junior dashboard, monthly vendor reconciliation, and named-student counselor lists for 2026-Q3. Add summer transportation hubs at Seaport High, East Harbor High, and the Airport Road transit center so students can reach bridge courses and certification labs. Set a Q3 operating goal to convert at least the same categories that drove this quarter’s progress: dual-credit posting, industry-certification completion, and math credit recovery.

periods.analysis: College and career readiness increased from 55.3% to 56.1%. It is improving but remains below the 60% target; posted credits and credential records need continued verification.
periods.recommendations: Have counselors reconcile outstanding dual-credit and certification records and follow up with students whose readiness evidence is incomplete.
